newsitem.title: USA: Upbeat Clinton to set agenda for G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Upbeat Clinton to set agenda for G7 summit.

text.p: An upbeat President Bill Clinton on Thursday sets out his agenda for this weekend's summit of industrialized nations, revelling in a robust U.S. economy that is the envy of his peers.

U.S. officials say Clinton will try to shift the focus of the Group of Seven summit away from traditional economic issues towards global challenges that are more understandable to Americans, like fighting the drug trade, terrorism and cementing global democracy.

In a speech delivered in Denver as the first of the foreign leaders arrives, Clinton will surely be remembering with some satisfaction the attacks he suffered from other G7 nations when he took over as president in 1993 at a time when massive U.S. budget deficits were seen as a threat to economic stability.
At the Denver summit, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, "We go in enjoying the benefits of a strong and robust economy."

In what one analyst described as a "gold era for the U.S. economy", unemployment is at its lowest level in nearly 24 years, the government budget deficit is small and shrinking, and inflation is low and stable.
Clinton will underline his country's strength at a time when European nations are battling high unemployment and Japan is emerging from years of economic woes.

Officials have detailed a packed agenda at the three days of talks starting on Friday and formally dubbed the "Summit of the Eight," where Russia's Boris Yeltsin will join the leaders of the G7 nations -- the United States, Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan.
The industrialized states are facing none of the financial crises that bedevilled them in the past and dominated their summits.
The G7 nations are scheduling just one hour of talks in Denver on purely economic matters -- on Saturday afternoon -- and that will be the only session to exclude Yeltsin.
In his speech just after 1 p.m. local (1900 GMT) on Thursday Clinton will argue that it is time to concentrate on "some of the new challenges we face in the post-Cold War era."

The one foreign policy issue accorded a separate session, on Saturday, is Bosnia. Washington has initiated a new drive to rebuild solid democratic institutions in the war-ravaged country before an international peace-keeping force is slated to leave in the middle of next year
With China poised to take control of Hong Kong in less than two weeks, the leaders are also expected to urge Beijing to honor promises to preserve the territory's autonomy, U.S. officials say.

Other foreign policy issues to be addressed include the Middle East peace process, differing approaches to Iran between Europe and the United States, ways to re-unite the divided island of Cyprus and wars in central Africa.

Many fear the agenda, also including economic issues like Japan's trade surplus, may be too broad to allow the leaders, meeting in what is known as the mile-high city, to have in-depth discussions of anything.
"The risk is the summit will be a mile high and a foot deep," Robert Hormats, Vice Chairman of Goldman Sachs International, said this week.
